questions.question: Name two spices that possess antimicrobial properties. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Name two spices that possess antimicrobial properties.
  • Clove and cinnamon possess antimicrobial properties.
  • Other acceptable examples include garlic, turmeric, black pepper and oregano.

questions.question: List the major steps involved in the processing of nutmeg. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• List the major steps involved in the processing of nutmeg.
  • Harvesting of mature fruits, followed by removal of the outer fleshy pericarp.
  • Separation of the mace (aril) from the nut; drying of mace separately.
  • Drying of the nut, cracking the shell, removal of the kernel, grading and packing.

questions.solution_html:
• Define cleaning of spices.
  • Cleaning is the unit operation of removing foreign and unwanted materials such as dust, soil, stones,
  • stalks, insects and other extraneous matter from spices.
  • It improves purity, safety and market quality.

questions.question: Define ginger. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define ginger.
  • Ginger is the underground stem (rhizome) of Zingiber officinale, a herbaceous plant belonging to the
  • family Zingiberaceae.
  • It is used as a spice for its pungent taste and characteristic aroma.

questions.question: What is black pepper? / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is black pepper?
  • Black pepper is the dried, usually unripe fruit (drupe/peppercorn) of Piper nigrum.
  • It is known for its pungency, mainly due to the alkaloid piperine.

questions.question: Differentiate between ethylene oxide treatment and conventional thermal treatment. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between ethylene oxide treatment and conventional thermal treatment.
  • Ethylene oxide treatment is a chemical fumigation process used to reduce microbial contamination;
  • it can be carried out at relatively low temperatures.
  • Thermal treatment uses heat (for example, steam or hot air) to destroy microorganisms.
  • Ethylene oxide requires strict control of residues, aeration and worker safety; heat treatment may
  • cause loss of volatile aroma compounds or colour changes.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Describe the different methods of drying cardamom. / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the different methods of drying cardamom.
  • Sun drying: Capsules are spread in a thin layer on clean drying floors or mats and turned
  • periodically. It is economical but depends on weather and may result in uneven drying or colour loss.
  • Flue-pipe drying: Capsules are dried in a chamber using heated air circulated through flue pipes. The
  • produce is not intended to come into direct contact with smoke or combustion gases.
  • Hot-air/mechanical drying: Controlled heated air is passed through trays or a drying chamber.
  • Temperature and airflow can be regulated, giving more uniform and faster drying.
  • Tray or cabinet drying: Cardamom is spread in shallow layers on trays and dried under controlled
  • conditions.
  • After drying, capsules are cooled, cleaned, graded and packed. Gentle drying helps retain the green
  • colour, aroma and essential oil.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the major factors affecting the rate of drying of spices. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the major factors affecting the rate of drying of spices.
  • Temperature of drying air: Higher temperature generally increases the rate of moisture evaporation,
  • but excessive heat can damage colour and volatile oils.
  • Relative humidity: Low relative humidity increases the moisture-removing capacity of air; high
  • humidity slows drying.
  • Air velocity and circulation: Faster, uniform airflow removes moist air from around the product and
  • improves drying.
  • Size, shape and surface area: Small pieces and thin layers dry faster because moisture has a shorter
  • path to move and more surface is exposed.
  • Initial moisture content and composition: High initial moisture generally requires longer drying; oil-
  • rich or dense tissues may dry more slowly.
  • Loading depth and arrangement: Thick layers and overcrowding restrict airflow and slow drying.
  • Nature of the product and pretreatment: Cutting, splitting or blanching (where suitable) can alter
  • moisture movement and drying time.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Describe the volatility, aroma and flavour characteristics of spice oils. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the volatility, aroma and flavour characteristics of spice oils.
  • Spice oils are mixtures of volatile aromatic compounds, commonly including terpenes, terpenoids,
  • aldehydes, phenols, alcohols and esters.
  • Volatility: These compounds evaporate readily, particularly during heating and prolonged exposure
  • to air. Volatility varies with molecular structure and boiling point.
  • Aroma: The characteristic smell of each spice is produced by its specific combination and proportion
  • of volatile compounds. Examples include eugenol in clove and cinnamaldehyde in cinnamon bark
  • oil.
  • Flavour: Spice oils contribute aroma and taste sensations such as warm, sweet, pungent, fresh or
  • herbal notes. Some compounds also contribute to pungency.
  • Storage: Heat, oxygen, light and moisture can cause evaporation or oxidation, reducing aroma
  • quality. Oils should be stored in tightly closed, suitable containers away from heat and light.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Differentiate between conventional extraction and supercritical carbon dioxide extraction of spice components. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between conventional extraction and supercritical carbon dioxide extraction of
  • spice components.
  • Principle: Conventional extraction uses liquid solvents (such as food-grade ethanol or other
  • permitted solvents) to dissolve target compounds. Supercritical CO₂ extraction uses carbon dioxide
  • above its critical temperature and pressure, where it has solvent-like properties.
  • Operating conditions: Conventional extraction is generally carried out at ordinary or moderately
  • elevated temperatures and solvent pressure. Supercritical extraction requires high-pressure
  • equipment and controlled temperature.
  • Selectivity: Conventional extraction selectivity depends on solvent polarity and process conditions.
  • Supercritical CO₂ selectivity can be adjusted by changing pressure and temperature; a co-solvent
  • may be used for more polar compounds.
  • Product quality: Supercritical CO₂ operates at relatively low temperatures and leaves no CO₂ residue
  • after depressurisation, helping retain heat-sensitive aroma compounds. Conventional extraction may
  • leave solvent residues unless adequately removed.
  • Cost and limitations: Conventional systems are usually simpler and less expensive but require
  • solvent recovery and residue control. Supercritical systems have high capital and operating costs but
  • can produce high-quality extracts.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Differentiate between flower spices and bud spices. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between flower spices and bud spices.
  • Flower spices are obtained from the flower or a part of an opened flower. Examples include saffron
  • (dried stigmas) and rose (petals, where used as a spice/flavouring).
  • Bud spices are obtained from unopened flower buds. The principal example is clove, which consists
  • of the dried unopened flower bud of Syzygium aromaticum.
  • Flower spices may include delicate reproductive parts such as stigma or petals, whereas bud spices
  • are harvested before the flower opens.
  • Their harvesting stage, morphology, processing and characteristic aroma differ.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Differentiate between the processing methods of saffron and cloves, highlighting their major processing operations. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between the processing methods of saffron and cloves, highlighting their major
  • processing operations.
  • Saffron: Flowers of Crocus sativus are harvested by hand, usually early in the day. The red stigmas
  • are carefully separated from the flowers.
  • The separated stigmas are dried under controlled conditions to develop the characteristic colour,
  • aroma and flavour, then cleaned, graded and packed in moisture- and light-protective packaging.
  • Cloves: Unopened flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum are harvested when they reach the
  • appropriate stage and show a characteristic colour change.
  • The stalks are separated as required, and buds are dried by sun or artificial drying until they become
  • brown and sufficiently dry. They are then cleaned, graded and packed.
  • Key difference: Saffron processing centres on delicate hand separation and careful drying of stigmas,
  • whereas clove processing involves harvesting and drying whole unopened flower buds.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the advantages and limitations of irradiation treatment of spices. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the advantages and limitations of irradiation treatment of spices.
  • Advantages: Irradiation reduces microbial load, including pathogenic and spoilage microorganisms,
  • and can control insects and pests.
  • It can be carried out with limited temperature rise, helping preserve heat-sensitive flavour and aroma
  • better than some heat treatments.
  • It can treat packaged products, reduce the need for chemical fumigants and extend storage life when
  • combined with good packaging and hygiene.
  • Limitations: Installation and operation require specialised, costly equipment, trained personnel and
  • regulatory approval.
  • The treatment does not replace good manufacturing practices and may not destroy all microbial
  • spores under every condition.
  • Excessive or unsuitable doses may affect sensory or chemical quality. Labelling and dose limits
  • must comply with applicable regulations.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: List the advantages of plastic packaging for spices. / [CO5] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• List the advantages of plastic packaging for spices.
  • Lightweight, flexible and convenient to handle and transport.
  • Can provide a good barrier to moisture and, depending on the polymer and laminate, oxygen and
  • aroma loss.
  • Helps protect spices from contamination, dust, insects and handling damage.
  • Can be heat-sealed to form secure packs and is available in different sizes and forms.
  • Transparent films allow product visibility; printed films provide branding and product information.
  • Generally economical and suitable for automated packaging. Barrier performance depends on the
  • type and thickness of plastic used.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the relationship between the chemical composition of spices and their functional properties in food preservation, flavouring and health promotion. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the relationship between the chemical composition of spices and their functional
  • properties in food preservation, flavouring and health promotion.
  • Spices contain essential oils, phenolic compounds, alkaloids, pigments, resins, pungent principles
  • and other phytochemicals. Their composition determines their characteristic sensory and functional
  • properties.
  • Food preservation – antimicrobial action: Certain phenolic and aromatic compounds inhibit bacteria,
  • yeasts and moulds. Examples include eugenol in clove, cinnamaldehyde in cinnamon and compounds in
  • garlic. Their effectiveness depends on concentration, food composition and the target microorganism.
  • Food preservation – antioxidant action: Phenolic compounds and pigments can scavenge free
  • radicals or slow oxidation of fats, helping delay rancidity and quality deterioration. Examples
  • include curcuminoids in turmeric and phenolic compounds in several herbs and spices.
  • Flavouring: Volatile essential-oil components provide characteristic aroma. Examples include
  • eugenol (clove), cinnamaldehyde (cinnamon), menthol (mint), and terpenes such as limonene (citrus
  • peel).
  • Taste and pungency: Piperine gives black pepper its pungency; gingerols and shogaols contribute to
  • ginger pungency; capsaicinoids give chilli its heat.
  • Colour: Curcumin gives turmeric its yellow colour; carotenoid pigments contribute red or orange
  • colour in chilli and paprika.
  • Health-related properties: Several spice constituents have been studied for antioxidant, anti-
  • inflammatory, digestive and other biological activities. For example, curcuminoids, gingerols and
  • capsaicin have been investigated for such effects.
  • The health effects of spices depend on dose, bioavailability and the overall diet. Spices are foods or
  • food ingredients and should not be presented as substitutes for medical treatment.
  • Conclusion: The chemical composition of each spice determines its aroma, taste, colour, antimicrobial
  • and antioxidant potential, making spices valuable in food formulation and quality preservation.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Describe the various factors affecting the storage stability and shelf life of spices. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the various factors affecting the storage stability and shelf life of spices.
  • Moisture content and water activity: High moisture encourages mould growth, insect activity, caking
  • and quality deterioration. Spices should be dried to safe moisture levels and protected from moisture
  • uptake.
  • Temperature: High storage temperatures accelerate loss of volatile oils, oxidation, colour changes
  • and deterioration. Cool storage helps preserve quality.
  • Relative humidity: High humidity can cause moisture absorption and mould growth; storage areas
  • should be dry and well ventilated.
  • Light: Light can degrade pigments and sensitive flavour compounds. Opaque or light-protective
  • packaging reduces exposure.
  • Oxygen: Oxygen promotes oxidation of essential oils, pigments and other constituents. Airtight
  • packaging and suitable oxygen-barrier materials help limit deterioration.
  • Packaging material: Packaging should protect against moisture, oxygen, light, insects and external
  • odours. Barrier properties and seal integrity are important.
  • Form of spice: Whole spices generally retain volatile oils and flavour longer than ground spices
  • because grinding increases exposed surface area.
  • Initial quality and microbial load: Proper harvesting, cleaning, drying and hygienic handling reduce
  • contamination and improve keeping quality.
  • Insects and pests: Insect infestation causes physical damage, contamination and loss of market value.
  • Sanitation, pest control and suitable packaging are necessary.
  • Storage conditions and handling: Clean, dry warehouses, pallets, protection from walls/floors, stock
  • rotation (FIFO/FEFO) and avoidance of strong-smelling materials help maintain quality.
  • Conclusion: Shelf life is maintained by controlling moisture, temperature, oxygen, light, pests and
  • contamination, together with appropriate packaging and good storage practices.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the mechanical methods of chilli drying in detail. / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the mechanical methods of chilli drying in detail.
  • Mechanical drying uses equipment to supply controlled heat and airflow, reducing dependence on
  • sunlight and weather.
  • Tray/cabinet drying: Clean chillies are spread in a uniform, shallow layer on perforated trays. Heated
  • air is circulated through the cabinet; trays may be rotated or rearranged to improve uniformity.
  • Hot-air or batch drying: Chillies are loaded into a drying chamber and heated air is passed over or
  • through the produce. Temperature, air velocity and drying time are controlled to reach the required
  • final moisture.
  • Continuous-belt drying: Chillies move on a perforated conveyor through zones of heated air.
  • Residence time, belt speed and air conditions are adjusted to obtain uniform drying in larger-scale
  • operations.
  • Fluidised-bed drying: In suitable systems and product sizes, upward-moving hot air suspends or
  • agitates the product, improving heat and mass transfer. It is less commonly used for whole large
  • chillies than for smaller particles or processed materials.
  • Pre-drying operations: Harvesting at proper maturity, sorting, removal of damaged pods and
  • cleaning are carried out. Chillies may be washed only when the process includes adequate
  • subsequent drying.
  • Process control: Excessively high temperature can cause colour degradation, loss of pungency/aroma
  • and surface hardening. Air temperature, humidity, airflow, loading depth and drying time must be
  • controlled.
  • Post-drying: Dried chillies are cooled, cleaned, graded and packed in moisture-resistant packaging.
  • They should be stored in a cool, dry place away from light and pests.
  • Advantages: Faster and more uniform drying, reduced dependence on weather, better process
  • control, reduced contamination risk and suitability for commercial-scale production.
  • Limitations: Higher equipment and energy costs; poor control may cause uneven drying, colour loss
  • or deterioration of volatile constituents.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Compare propylene oxide treatment with ethylene oxide and steam sterilization for spice decontamination. / [CO4] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare propylene oxide treatment with ethylene oxide and steam sterilization for spice
  • decontamination.
  • Propylene oxide (PO): A chemical fumigant used to reduce microbial contamination in spices. It
  • reacts with cellular constituents and can be effective at relatively low temperatures. Residues and
  • reaction products must be controlled, and use is subject to regulatory approval.
  • Ethylene oxide (EtO): A gaseous chemical sterilant/fumigant with strong antimicrobial activity. It can
  • penetrate packaged or bulk products and is used at relatively low temperatures, but it presents significant
  • worker-safety and residue concerns. Adequate aeration and strict regulatory controls are essential.
  • Steam sterilization: Uses moist heat to inactivate microorganisms. It avoids chemical fumigant residues
  • and can be effective when time and temperature are properly controlled.
  • Effect on quality: PO and EtO may better preserve heat-sensitive volatile components than high-
  • temperature steam, but chemical residues and safety risks are concerns. Steam may cause loss of
  • volatile oils, changes in colour, flavour or texture if treatment is too severe.
  • Operational considerations: Chemical fumigation requires gas-tight equipment, monitoring, trained
  • operators, aeration and residue testing. Steam treatment requires controlled steam exposure, followed
  • by drying to prevent moisture-related spoilage.
  • Safety and regulation: The acceptability and permitted use of PO and EtO vary by jurisdiction and
  • food category; they must not be assumed to be permitted. Applicable national regulations and
  • maximum residue requirements must be followed. Steam is generally preferred where it can achieve
  • the required microbial reduction without unacceptable quality loss.
  • Comparison summary: PO and EtO are low-temperature chemical decontamination methods with
  • residue and occupational-safety concerns; steam is a physical heat treatment with no fumigant residue
  • but may affect heat-sensitive spice quality.
